opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's been one of the really exciting stories in robotics over the last several years. If you'd told me ten years ago that we'd have four-legged robots trotting up rocky hillsides, climbing stairs, and recovering when someone kicks them, I would have been skeptical. But it's happened, and I think it's worth unpacking why, because it tells us something about where robotics is easy and where it's still very hard.

A few things came together. The first is hardware. Motors got much better: lighter, more powerful, and with good torque control. Battery technology improved, and the cost of these platforms dropped dramatically. Companies like Boston Dynamics showed what was possible, and now you can buy a quadruped from several companies for the price of a used car, so many more labs can experiment.

The second, and I think the bigger factor, is simulation combined with reinforcement learning. Locomotion is a problem that's well suited to simulation. The robot is mostly interacting with the ground through its feet, and the physics of that, rigid bodies, contacts, gravity, can be modeled reasonably well. So researchers can run thousands of virtual robots in parallel on GPUs, essentially years of experience compressed into hours, and let the robots learn by trial and error.

The key trick that made this transfer to the real world is what's called domain randomization. You don't simulate one perfect world; you vary friction, mass, motor strength, terrain shape, sensor noise, delays, and so on. The policy that emerges has to be robust to all of that variation, so when you put it on the real robot, reality looks like just one more variation it's already seen. Groups at ETH Zurich, Berkeley, CMU, and elsewhere showed that you could train entirely in simulation and deploy on real hardware with surprisingly little fine-tuning.

And interestingly, a lot of this works with proprioception alone, the robot's sense of its own joint angles and forces, almost like walking with your eyes closed. It feels the ground and adapts. Adding vision helps for anticipating stairs or gaps, but the core robustness came from learning to react.

Now, here's the caveat I always emphasize. People see these videos and conclude that robots are about to do everything. But locomotion is fundamentally different from manipulation. When a robot walks, it just needs to keep its body upright and moving. When a robot picks up an object, say, a crumpled shirt or a glass of water or a tangled cable, the physics of contact is far more complex and much harder to simulate accurately. Tiny differences in friction or shape matter enormously. So the sim-to-real approach that's worked so well for legs hasn't transferred nearly as cleanly to hands. That's what I call the gap between the robot dog doing backflips and the robot that can reliably clear your dinner table. We're making progress, but that second problem is much, much harder.

r001.rationale: The response credits improved hardware, simulation, reinforcement learning, and domain randomization, but does not identify combining model predictive control with deep learning.

fable-5.1.text:
Sure. The big thing to understand is that locomotion turned out to be a much more tractable problem than people expected, and the reason is simulation. Walking is a problem where the physics is relatively well understood. You have rigid bodies, joints, contacts with the ground, and we have simulators that can model that reasonably faithfully. So you can put a four-legged robot into a simulated environment, randomize the terrain, randomize the friction, randomize the mass of the legs a bit, and run millions of trials in parallel on a GPU. The robot falls over a million times in simulation, and that costs nothing. Then you take the policy you learned and transfer it onto the real robot, and it works surprisingly well. That's what people call sim-to-real transfer, and for legged locomotion it has been remarkably successful.

The other piece is that the hardware got good. The actuators from companies like Boston Dynamics, Unitree, ANYbotics, they're fast, they're compliant, and they have good proprioceptive sensing, so the robot can feel what's happening at the feet without needing to see it. A lot of these controllers barely use vision at all. They rely on the sense of where the joints are and how much torque they're applying, and that turns out to be enough to recover from a slip or a step onto a rock.

I want to be careful here, though, because I think people watch those videos and extrapolate too far. Legs on terrain is a problem with a lot of favorable structure. Mistakes are recoverable, the state space is relatively low-dimensional, and the simulator matches reality well enough. Manipulation, which is what I work on, is almost the opposite on every count. When a robot's gripper touches an object, the contact dynamics are chaotic, the friction is unpredictable, objects deform, and the simulators just don't match the real world the way they do for walking. So the lesson of legged robots isn't that robots are about to do everything. The lesson is that when you can simulate a problem well, you can make astonishing progress. The hard part is figuring out which problems those are.

r001.rationale: The response credits simulation-based learning and sim-to-real transfer, along with improved hardware and proprioception. It does not identify combining model predictive control with deep learning.

astra-6.text:
I think what’s exciting is that it’s a combination of advances. The hardware has gotten much better—the motors, the sensors, the ability to control the forces at each foot. But there have also been substantial advances in the algorithms that coordinate all of that.

One particularly powerful approach is to train these systems in simulation. You can have a robot try to walk over uneven terrain many, many times, including falling over, without breaking an expensive piece of hardware. And you can vary the conditions: make the ground more slippery, change the slopes, introduce disturbances. The challenge is then getting what it learns in simulation to work on the physical robot, where things are never quite as clean as they are in the model.

And the feedback is crucial. It’s not simply executing a predetermined sequence of steps. It’s continually sensing what’s happening and adjusting. If a foot lands somewhere unexpected, the controller has to respond quickly enough to maintain balance. That combination of better hardware, learning, and rapid feedback is what makes these movements possible.

r001.rationale: The response discusses simulation training, algorithms, and rapid feedback, but it does not identify combining model predictive control with deep learning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think what’s striking is that it’s a combination of advances. You’ve got better actuators, better sensors, more computation onboard, and much better control algorithms. The robot has to continually estimate where its body is, where its feet are, and how the ground is responding, and then make adjustments very quickly.

Learning has also become an important part of that. You can train a controller in simulation, expose it to lots of different conditions, and then transfer it to the physical robot. But that transfer is a challenge, because the real world never behaves exactly like your simulator. A foothold might slip, or the ground might give way.

So I wouldn’t attribute it to a single breakthrough. It’s the integration of mechanics, control, and learning—and getting those systems to cope with uncertainty—that makes the progress so impressive.

r001.rationale: The response describes combining control algorithms with learning, but does not identify model predictive control or deep learning.
